title: Marketing Management
summary: Marketing is a social process through which individuals and groups obtain what they need and want by creating, offering and freely exchanging products and services of value with others. This chapter covers the features and functions of marketing, marketing philosophies, marketing versus selling, and the marketing mix: product (branding, packaging, labelling), price, place (channels and physical distribution) and promotion (advertising, personal selling, sales promotion and public relations).

notes.heading: Meaning and Features of Marketing
notes.html:
Market traditionally means a place where buyers and sellers meet; in modern marketing, it means the set of actual and potential buyers of a product. Marketing is a social process by which people obtain what they need and want through creating, offering and freely exchanging products of value. Marketing management means planning, organising, directing and controlling marketing activities to achieve exchanges with target markets.

Features:

  1. Needs and wants – marketing helps individuals and organisations satisfy their needs and wants.
  2. Creating a market offering – a complete offer (product, price, place, features) is developed for the target market.
  3. Customer value – buyers choose the offering that gives them the greatest value for money.
  4. Exchange mechanism – marketing works through exchange of products for money; conditions: at least two parties, something of value, communication and freedom to accept or reject.

What can be marketed: physical products, services, ideas, persons, places, experiences, events, organisations.

notes.heading: Functions of Marketing
notes.html:
1. Gathering and analysing market information – identifying customer needs and opportunities (e.g. SWOT analysis).
  2. Marketing planning – developing plans to increase sales and market share.
  3. Product designing and development – designing an attractive product suited to customers.
  4. Standardisation and grading – standardisation ensures uniform quality (e.g. ISI, Agmark); grading classifies products on quality, size etc. (mainly agricultural produce).
  5. Packaging and labelling – protecting and identifying the product.
  6. Branding – giving the product a distinctive identity.
  7. Customer support services – after-sales service, handling complaints, credit services.
  8. Pricing of products – deciding the price based on cost, demand and competition.
  9. Promotion – informing and persuading customers through advertising, personal selling, sales promotion and publicity.
  10. Physical distribution – moving goods from producers to consumers.
  11. Transportation – physical movement of goods.
  12. Storage or warehousing – storing goods to bridge the gap between production and consumption.

notes.heading: Marketing Mix: Product, Branding, Packaging, Labelling
notes.html:
Marketing mix is the set of marketing tools a firm uses to pursue its objectives: the 4 Ps – Product, Price, Place, Promotion.

Product – anything of value offered to the market to satisfy needs: goods, services, ideas. A product is a bundle of utilities (functional, psychological, social).

Branding – giving a name, sign, symbol or design to a product. Brand name = verbal part; brand mark = symbol; trademark = legally registered brand or part of it.

  • Advantages to marketers: helps product differentiation, helps in advertising and display, enables differential pricing, eases introduction of new products.
  • Advantages to customers: easy identification, ensures quality, status symbol.
  • Characteristics of a good brand name: short, easy to pronounce, spell and remember; suggests product benefits; distinctive; adaptable to packing and labelling; versatile for new products; capable of being registered; long-lasting.

Packaging – designing and producing the container or wrapper. Levels: primary (immediate container, e.g. toothpaste tube), secondary (additional layer, e.g. cardboard box), transportation (for storage and transport, e.g. carton of 100 tubes). Functions: product identification, product protection, facilitates use, product promotion. Importance: rising health and sanitation standards, self-service outlets, innovation opportunity, product differentiation.

Labelling – the slip or tag attached to a product giving information. Functions: describe the product and specify contents; identification of product or brand; grading; help in promotion; providing information required by law (e.g. MRP, date of manufacture and expiry, statutory warnings).

notes.heading: Price: Factors Affecting Price Determination
notes.html:
Price is the amount of money paid by buyers for a product. It is the only element of the marketing mix that generates revenue.

  1. Product cost – price should cover fixed, variable and semi-variable costs plus a fair profit.
  2. Utility and demand – the price cannot exceed the utility to the buyer; elastic demand calls for a lower price.
  3. Extent of competition – prices close to competitors' when competition is high.
  4. Government and legal regulations – government may fix prices of essential products (e.g. some medicines).
  5. Pricing objectives – profit maximisation, market share leadership, surviving competition, product quality leadership.
  6. Marketing methods used – distribution system, quality of salesmen, advertising, packaging, credit and after-sales services affect price.

notes.heading: Place: Channels of Distribution and Physical Distribution
notes.html:
Channels of distribution are the individuals and firms (middlemen) involved in transferring goods from producer to consumer.

  • Zero level (direct): Manufacturer → Customer (e.g. door-to-door sales, online store, company outlets).
  • One level: Manufacturer → Retailer → Customer (e.g. cars, consumer durables).
  • Two level: Manufacturer → Wholesaler → Retailer → Customer (most common for consumer goods).
  • Three level: Manufacturer → Agent → Wholesaler → Retailer → Customer.

Factors determining choice of channel: product-related (perishability, value, technical nature); company characteristics (financial strength, desire for control); competitive factors; market factors (size of market, geographic concentration, quantity purchased); environmental factors (e.g. economic conditions, legal constraints).

Physical distribution covers all activities required to move goods physically from manufacturer to customer. Components:

  1. Order processing – accurate and speedy processing of orders.
  2. Transportation – moving goods; mode chosen on cost, speed, nature of product.
  3. Warehousing – storing goods; creates time utility.
  4. Inventory control – maintaining an optimum level of stock.

notes.heading: Promotion: Advertising and Personal Selling
notes.html:
Promotion mix = advertising, personal selling, sales promotion and public relations.

Advertising – any paid form of non-personal presentation and promotion of ideas, goods or services by an identified sponsor. Features: paid form, impersonality, identified sponsor. Merits: mass reach, enhances customer satisfaction and confidence, expressiveness, economy (low cost per person reached). Limitations: less forceful, lack of feedback, inflexibility, low effectiveness due to clutter.

Objections to advertising and answers: adds to cost (but increases demand and lowers per-unit cost); undermines social values (but informs buyers); confuses buyers (but buyers can compare); encourages sale of inferior products (quality is relative); some ads are in bad taste (taste differs; ASCI regulates).

Personal selling – oral presentation in a conversation with one or more prospective customers for the purpose of making sales. Features: personal form, development of relationship. Role: for businessmen – effective promotional tool, flexible, minimises wastage, creates consumer attention, builds lasting relations, helps introduce new products; for customers – identifies needs, gives latest market information, expert advice; for society – converts latent demand, generates employment, career opportunities, mobility of sales people, product standardisation.

BasisAdvertisingPersonal Selling
FormImpersonalPersonal, face-to-face
FlexibilityInflexible; same message to allFlexible; adjusted to each customer
ReachLarge number of peopleLimited number of people
Cost per personLowHigh
FeedbackSlow, difficult to measureImmediate

notes.heading: Promotion: Sales Promotion and Public Relations
notes.html:
Sales promotion – short-term incentives to encourage immediate purchase. Merits: attention value, useful in new product launch, synergy in total promotional efforts. Limitations: reflects crisis (frequent use suggests the firm cannot sell), spoils product image.

Common sales promotion techniques:

  • Rebate – sale at reduced price for a limited period to clear stock.
  • Discount – sale at less than list price (e.g. 20% off).
  • Refund – refunding part of the price on proof of purchase.
  • Product combination – another product given free with the main product.
  • Quantity gift – extra quantity free (e.g. 20% extra).
  • Instant draws and assigned gifts – scratch cards with instant prizes.
  • Lucky draw – draw of coupons for prizes.
  • Usable benefit – e.g. shopping vouchers worth ₹500 on purchase above ₹5,000.
  • Full finance at 0% – easy instalments without interest.
  • Sampling – free samples to potential customers.
  • Contests – competitive events requiring skill.

Public relations – managing communication between the organisation and its publics to build goodwill. Role: press relations, product publicity, corporate communication, lobbying, counselling. Publicity is non-paid, non-personal communication through news in mass media.

mcqs.q: A detergent company uses biodegradable packaging and runs campaigns on water conservation along with selling its product. Which marketing philosophy does it follow?
mcqs.explanation: Combining customer satisfaction with the long-term welfare of society is the societal marketing concept.

mcqs.q: The cardboard box in which a bottle of perfume is placed is an example of:
mcqs.explanation: An additional layer protecting the immediate container is secondary packaging.

mcqs.q: 'Buy a 1 kg pack of coffee and get a coffee mug free.' Which sales promotion technique is this?
mcqs.explanation: Giving another product free with the main product is product combination.

mcqs.q: Which element of the marketing mix is the only one that generates revenue?
mcqs.explanation: Price brings in revenue; the other elements involve costs.

mcqs.q: A fashion brand sells its clothes only through its own website and company-owned stores. Which channel is used?
mcqs.explanation: Selling directly to customers without middlemen is a zero level (direct) channel.

mcqs.q: The government fixed the maximum retail price of certain life-saving drugs. Which factor affecting price determination is this?
mcqs.explanation: Price control by the government falls under government and legal regulations.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of advertising?
mcqs.explanation: Advertising lacks immediate feedback; that is a feature of personal selling.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): Marketing has a wider scope than selling.
Reason (R): Marketing starts before production by identifying customer needs and continues after sale.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Because marketing covers activities before, during and after sale, its scope is wider than selling.

mcqs.q: A label on a juice pack mentions 'Best before 6 months from manufacture' and MRP. Which function of labelling is this mainly?
mcqs.explanation: Information like MRP and expiry date is mandatory, so it is providing information required by law.

mcqs.q: A company believes that customers will buy products that are widely available and cheap, so it concentrates on mass production. Which concept is this?
mcqs.explanation: Focus on availability and affordability through mass production is the production concept.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): Frequent use of sales promotion may harm the image of a product.
Reason (R): Customers may feel that the product is of poor quality or not selling well.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Repeated offers make buyers suspect quality or a crisis, which explains the damage to image.

mcqs.q: A newspaper published a news story about a firm's free health camp in villages without the firm paying for it. This is:
mcqs.explanation: Non-paid, non-personal communication through news media is publicity, a part of public relations.

questions.q: What is meant by marketing mix?
questions.answerHtml: Marketing mix is the set of marketing tools – product, price, place and promotion – that a firm uses to achieve its marketing objectives in the target market.

questions.q: Name the level of packaging which refers to the immediate container of a product.
State any three functions of labelling.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Describes the product and specifies its contents – tells the customer about usage, ingredients and cautions.
  2. Identification of the product or brand – helps customers pick out the product from others.
  3. Providing information required by law – e.g. MRP, net quantity, date of manufacture and expiry, statutory warnings.

Starting pointBegins before productionBegins after production

questions.q: Explain any four factors affecting the determination of price of a product.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Product cost – price must cover the total cost of producing, distributing and selling the product, plus a reasonable profit.
  2. Utility and demand – the buyer will not pay more than the utility derived; if demand is elastic, a lower price is fixed.
  3. Extent of competition – where competition is high, prices are kept close to those of competitors.
  4. Government and legal regulations – the government may fix or control prices of essential goods to protect the public.

questions.q: Explain the components of physical distribution.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Order processing – accurate and quick processing of orders ensures timely supply and customer satisfaction.
  2. Transportation – physical movement of goods from the place of production to the place of consumption; the mode depends on the nature, cost and urgency.
  3. Warehousing – storing goods until they are needed; it creates time utility and smooths supply.
  4. Inventory control – maintaining the right level of stock to balance customer service and cost of holding stock.

questions.q: Explain any six characteristics of a good brand name.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Short, easy to pronounce, spell and remember – e.g. a two-syllable name.
  2. Suggests the product's benefits and qualities – the name should relate to its function.
  3. Distinctive – it should stand apart from competitors' names.
  4. Adaptable to packing and labelling – it should fit different media and package sizes.
  5. Versatile – it should accommodate new products added to the product line.
  6. Capable of being registered and legally protected – so that others cannot copy it.

A good brand name should also have staying power, i.e. it should not become outdated quickly.

questions.q: ZestFit, a new brand of fitness bands, (a) gave free trial bands to gym trainers, (b) ran TV commercials during cricket matches, (c) appointed trained executives to demonstrate the bands at malls and answer customers' questions, and (d) got a newspaper to publish a story about its free fitness camps. Identify the elements of promotion mix in each case and explain any two of them.
questions.answerHtml:
Identification:

  • (a) Sales promotion – sampling (free trial bands).
  • (b) Advertising – paid TV commercials.
  • (c) Personal selling – face-to-face demonstration by trained executives.
  • (d) Public relations – publicity through a news story.

Explanation:

  1. Advertising – any paid form of non-personal presentation and promotion of goods, services or ideas by an identified sponsor. It reaches a large audience at a low cost per person, but it is inflexible and lacks immediate feedback.
  2. Personal selling – oral presentation in a conversation with prospective customers for the purpose of making sales. It is flexible, gives immediate feedback and helps build lasting relationships with customers.
